title: Monopolies
objective: After this level you can explain what a monopoly is and why governments limit them.
summary: A monopoly is one seller of something with no substitute, shielded by barriers to entry. It sells less at a higher price, so laws limit it: Standard Oil was broken up in 1911.

cards.headline: The board game Monopoly began as an economics lesson.
cards.body: It grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Lizzie Magie patented in 1904 to teach economic ideas about land and rent. Real monopolies are a lot less fun to play against.

cards.headline: One seller, no substitute
cards.body: A monopoly is a market with a single supplier of something that has no substitute. It can set its price without fear of competitors. What keeps rivals out? Barriers to entry: legal, technological or market forces that stop newcomers. Behind those walls, big profits no longer pull in Level 46's rivals, so nothing drags the price down.

cards.headline: Less stuff, higher prices
cards.body: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly sells a smaller quantity at a higher price, so buyers lose out. It can get lazy, too: with no rival to fear, it can keep making the same old products in the same old way. In 1935, economist John Hicks summed it up: "The best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life."

cards.fact: Standard Oil once refined 90 to 95 percent of America's oil. Then came the breakup.
cards.context: That was its share by 1880. In 1890, the Sherman Act outlawed monopolizing a market, and in 1911 the US Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil broken up into separate companies. Governments limit monopolies to protect what Level 46 showed: competition is what keeps prices down and quality up.

A board game about banks
options.rationale: The game is named after the idea, not the other way round.

options.label: A single seller of something with no substitute

questions.explanation: A monopoly is the exclusive possession of a market by a supplier of a product or service that has no substitute.

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market, what does a monopoly usually do?

options.label: Sells more at a lower price
options.rationale: That is what competition tends to do.

options.label: Sells less at a higher price
Sells the same amount at the same price
options.rationale: Without rivals, it can charge more and sell less.

options.label: Gives its product away to win customers
options.rationale: With no rivals, it has no need to.

questions.explanation: Without rivals, a monopoly sells a lower quantity at a higher price, and consumers lose out.

questions.prompt: Why do governments use laws like the Sherman Act to limit monopolies?

options.label: To set every price themselves
options.rationale: Antitrust laws protect competition; they do not set prices.

options.label: To help the biggest firm grow faster
options.rationale: They do the opposite: they stop one firm dominating.

options.label: To protect the competition that keeps prices down and quality up
To collect more tax from large companies
options.rationale: That is a job for tax law, not antitrust law.

questions.explanation: Competition pushes businesses to run efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up. Antitrust laws protect it.
